title: Overview and justification
body:
This advanced course is about the deep end of finding and using sources: judging what you find with rigour, and reaching past the obvious to find what a quick search misses. It assumes you can already build and run a search. By the end you will be able to evaluate sources against explicit criteria, extend a search across databases and citation trails, and refine a search for precision and recall.

At this level, a competent search is not the finish line. The sources you choose, and the ones you discard with reasons, shape the quality of everything you write. Searching well is a scholarly judgement, and it is one your markers and, later, your professional field will expect you to defend.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this course, you will be able to:

_items.text: evaluate sources rigorously against explicit criteria and justify which to use
extend a search beyond the discovery service using databases and citation searching
refine a search for precision and recall and iterate the strategy deliberately.

title: In real academic practice
body: Finding and using sources well is the engine of independent research. Every literature review, every dissertation, every evidence-based argument you make rests on a search that was wide enough to be fair and sharp enough to be useful, and on sources you judged rather than simply collected. These are the habits that separate competent work from genuinely scholarly work, and they carry straight into research and professional practice.

title: Signpost
body: The course has three short lessons. First, evaluating sources with rigour: judging quality against explicit criteria. Second, extending your search: reaching past the discovery service into databases and citation trails. Third, refining for precision: controlling what a search returns and iterating it deliberately. Work through them in order; each builds on the one before.
instruction: Work through the three lessons in order.

title: Course instructions
body:
Start and finish with a confidence check. Before the lessons, you'll rate how confident you feel about each part of this topic. You'll rate the same statements again at the end, so you can see what has changed. Your ratings are yours: they aren't marked and no one else sees them.

The activities in the lessons are for practice. Questions, examples and reflective prompts are there to help you think, and they don't count towards passing. Reflective prompts are private and optional.

The test at the end is the one that counts. To complete the course you need to take the final test and score at least 70%. You can retake it.

title: How this course works
body:
The examples and activities in this course use invented people, authors and sources to show how things work. Unless we say otherwise, any name, citation or reference you meet in an example is fictional.

Where a lesson draws on real work, you'll find it listed under Lesson Sources at the bottom of that page. Every real source used in the course is gathered under Course Sources at the end.

title: Orientation
body: Finding a source is the easy part. The judgement that matters at this level is deciding whether a source is good enough, and good for what, before you build an argument on it. This lesson makes that judgement explicit, turning a vague sense that a source feels trustworthy into criteria you can apply and defend.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You already locate sources competently, so this lesson does not revisit how to search. It sharpens the appraisal that should follow every search: weighing source type, currency, authority and relevance against the specific question you are asking, and justifying the sources you keep and the ones you set aside.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: appraise a source against explicit criteria of currency, authority and relevance
judge how a source's type bears on whether and how to use it
justify which sources in {{context}} to draw on and which to set aside.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Evaluating a source means weighing it against explicit criteria rather than trusting a first impression. Four criteria do most of the work. Source type tells you what kind of evidence you are holding and what it can fairly support. Currency asks whether the date of publication still matters for your question. Authority asks who produced the source, on what standing, and whether it was reviewed. Relevance asks how directly it answers the exact question you are asking.

These criteria are not a checklist to tick and forget. They trade off against each other, and the weighting depends on your question. A recent, highly relevant blog post may still lose to an older peer-reviewed study when authority is what your argument needs. Evaluating well means naming that trade-off and defending the call.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of a source you used recently without really appraising it. Run it through the four criteria now: source type, currency, authority, relevance. Would it still earn its place?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: Evaluating sources with rigour means weighing them against explicit criteria, not a first impression: source type for what the evidence can support, currency for whether the date still matters, authority for who stands behind it, and relevance for how directly it answers your question. You can now appraise a source against these criteria, judge how its type bears on its use, and justify the sources you keep and discard. The next lesson widens the net, extending a search past the discovery service.

title: Orientation
body: A discovery service is a powerful front door, but it is only a front door. At this level, treating the first page of library results as the whole literature is the commonest way a search falls short. This lesson is about reaching past that door: into subject databases and along the citation trails that connect the work in your field.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You can already run a solid discovery-service search. The step up here is coverage: recognising what that search leaves out, and using databases and citation searching to close the gap, so that what you find is wide enough to be fair to the debate.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: explain why a discovery-service search alone leaves gaps in coverage
use subject databases to extend a search into indexed, specialist coverage
follow citations forward and back in {{context}} to extend the reach of a search.

title: Concept: definition
body:
A discovery service searches broadly across what your library holds, which makes it an excellent start and a poor finish. It favours breadth over depth, under-indexes specialist literature, and ranks by relevance rules you do not control. Extending a search means going where it cannot reach.

Two moves do most of this. Subject databases index the specialist literature of a field in depth, with controlled vocabulary and filters a general search lacks. Citation searching follows the links between works: backwards, through a paper's reference list to what it was built on, and forwards, through a citation index to later work that cites it. Together they turn a flat list of results into a map of a field's conversation.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think about a recent search where you stopped at the library results. What might a subject database or a citation trail have added? Name one source you may have missed.
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: A discovery-service search is a starting point, not the whole library: it favours breadth, under-indexes specialist work, and ranks by rules you do not set. You can now explain why it leaves gaps, use subject databases to reach indexed specialist coverage, and follow citations backwards and forwards to map a field's conversation. The next lesson sharpens the search itself, controlling precision and recall.

title: Orientation
body: Reaching widely is half the craft; the other half is control. A wide search that returns thousands of loosely related results is no more useful than a narrow one that misses the best work. This lesson is about steering a search deliberately, so you find enough without drowning, and treating that steering as a cycle you repeat rather than a single try.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You can already run a search and read its results. Here you take command of what it returns: combining terms with Boolean logic, tightening with phrases and truncation, narrowing with limiters, and balancing precision against recall as a judgement you revisit with each pass.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: use Boolean logic with phrase and truncation operators to control a search
apply limiters to balance precision against recall
refine a search strategy in {{context}} deliberately as an iterative cycle.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Every search balances two things. Recall is how much of the relevant material you capture; precision is how little irrelevant material you wade through to get it. Push for one and you usually lose the other, so refining a search means choosing the balance your task needs and adjusting it as you go.

The controls are few and powerful. Boolean operators combine terms: AND narrows, OR widens, NOT excludes. Quotation marks fix a phrase so the words stay together. Truncation, usually an asterisk, catches a word's variants from one stem. Limiters filter the results by date, source type, peer review and more. None of these is a single correct setting; you run the search, read what comes back, and refine. A search is a draft you revise, not a question you ask once.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Take a search you ran recently. How would you rebuild it with Boolean operators, a phrase, truncation and one limiter? Would you aim for more recall or more precision, and why?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: Refining a search means steering the balance between recall, how much relevant material you capture, and precision, how little irrelevant material you sift. You can now combine terms with Boolean logic, fix phrases and truncate stems, apply limiters to tune that balance, and treat refinement as an iterative cycle rather than a single pass. With evaluation, reach and precision together, you can run a search that is both fair and sharp, and defend every choice in it.

title: In real academic practice
body: From here, these habits are the foundation of independent research. Each literature review you scope, each database you search rather than settle for the first results, each source you weigh and justify, is this craft at work. It is also what research and professional practice reward: the ability to find the evidence that matters, judge it, and stand behind the choices you made.

title: Course Sources
instruction: This course draws on the following source.

_items.title: See pages 95 to 112 of Chapter 7, 'Research: Developing Effective Search Strategies', of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: Four criteria for judging a source
body: Four criteria do the real work of evaluating a source. Read each one and notice the question it asks.
instruction: Read through the cards below.

_items.title: Source type
_items.subtitle: What kind of evidence is this?
_items.text: A peer-reviewed study, a textbook, a news article and a blog post carry very different weight. The type tells you what the source can fairly support, and what it cannot.

_items.title: Currency
_items.subtitle: Does the date still matter?
_items.text: For a fast-moving field, a five-year-old finding may be out of date; for a foundational idea, age is no fault. Judge currency against your question, not by the calendar alone.

_items.title: Authority
_items.subtitle: Who stands behind it?
_items.text: Ask who produced the source, on what expertise, and whether it was reviewed or published by a body with standing. Authority is about warranted trust, not reputation alone.

_items.title: Relevance
_items.subtitle: Does it answer your question?
_items.text: A strong source on a nearby topic is still the wrong source. Relevance asks how directly the work speaks to the exact question you are asking.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two researchers each find a source for the same question and must decide whether to use it.

{{learner-a}} finds a recent, well-written online article that states the claim clearly, and uses it as evidence. It is current and easy to read, so it seems ideal. But {{learner-a}} has not asked what type of source it is or who stands behind it. It is a news piece summarising someone else's work, with no review and no named expertise. The appraisal stopped at readability.

{{learner-b}} finds the same article and runs it through the criteria. It is current and relevant, but its type is journalism, not research, and its authority is thin for a technical claim. {{learner-b}} traces it back to the peer-reviewed study it summarises and uses that instead, noting that the news piece is useful only for context. The weaker source is set aside, with a reason.

Both found a usable-looking source. Only {{learner-b}} judged it against explicit criteria, and could justify the choice.

title: Practical guidance
displayTitle: Checklist: How to appraise a source
body: Run every source you are tempted to use through these questions.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Have I named the source type and asked what it can fairly support?
Have I judged currency against my question, not just the publication date?
Have I checked who produced it, on what expertise, and whether it was reviewed?
Have I asked how directly it answers my exact question, not a nearby one?
Have I named the trade-off when criteria pull in different directions?
Can I justify, in a sentence, why I kept this source or set it aside?

title: Formative check: appraising against criteria
displayTitle: What best describes evaluating a source against explicit criteria?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What best describes evaluating a source against explicit criteria?

_items.text: Weighing source type, currency, authority and relevance against your question, and defending the call.
_items.feedback: Yes. That is a rigorous appraisal rather than a first impression.

_items.text: Choosing the source that is most recent and easiest to read.
_items.feedback: Recency and readability are only part of currency; they do not settle type, authority or relevance.

_items.text: Trusting any source that appears in the library catalogue.
_items.feedback: Being in the catalogue is not an appraisal; you still have to weigh the source.

_items.text: Collecting as many sources as possible so the bibliography looks full.
_items.feedback: Quantity is not quality; evaluation is about judging each source, not counting them.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Evaluation weighs explicit criteria against your question and defends the choice.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option that weighs several criteria against your question.
_incorrect.final: Evaluating a source means weighing type, currency, authority and relevance against your question, and justifying the call, not picking by recency, catalogue presence or count.

title: Formative check: the rigorous appraisal
displayTitle: In the worked example, what made the second researcher's appraisal rigorous rather than impressionistic?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What made the second researcher's appraisal rigorous?

_items.text: They weighed the source's type and authority, not just its recency and readability, and traced it to the study it summarised.
_items.feedback: Yes. They judged against criteria and acted on the judgement.

_items.text: They read the article more carefully than the first researcher.
_items.feedback: Care in reading is not the same as appraising against criteria.

_items.text: They preferred the article because it was clearly written.
_items.feedback: Clear writing is readability, which is exactly what the weaker appraisal stopped at.

_items.text: They used the most recent source they could find.
_items.feedback: Recency alone does not make an appraisal rigorous; type and authority mattered here.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Weighing type and authority, and tracing the claim to its source, is a rigorous appraisal.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for what the second researcher weighed beyond how the article read.
_incorrect.final: The appraisal was rigorous because it weighed source type and authority, not just recency and readability, and traced the claim back to the peer-reviewed study.

title: Formative check: justifying a choice
displayTitle: You are choosing between two sources in {{context}}. Which approach shows the rigorous evaluation this lesson describes?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which approach shows rigorous evaluation when choosing between two sources?

_items.text: Weigh each against source type, currency, authority and relevance, then justify which you keep and which you set aside.
_items.feedback: Yes. In {{context}}, that explicit, defensible appraisal is the point.

_items.text: Keep whichever source is more recent, whatever its type or authority.
_items.feedback: Currency is one criterion among four; recency alone does not justify a choice.

_items.text: Keep both, since more sources always strengthen an argument.
_items.feedback: Keeping everything avoids the judgement; evaluation means choosing with reasons.

_items.text: Keep the one that is easier to read and quote.
_items.feedback: Ease of reading is not a criterion for the quality or fit of a source.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, weighing all four criteria and justifying the choice is rigorous evaluation.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option that weighs the criteria and justifies the decision.
_incorrect.final: In {{context}}, rigorous evaluation weighs type, currency, authority and relevance and justifies which source to keep, rather than deciding by recency, count or readability.

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: Extending a search, stage by stage
body: Extending a search means moving outward from the discovery service in deliberate stages. Reveal each stage to see what it adds.
instruction: Select each stage to reveal how the search widens.

_items.title: Discovery service
_items.body: The library front door: broad, convenient, and ranked by rules you do not control. A good place to begin and a poor place to stop.

_items.title: Subject databases
_items.body: The indexed, specialist literature of your field, with controlled vocabulary and filters a general search lacks. This is where depth lives.

_items.title: Citation searching, backwards
_items.body: Follow a key paper's reference list to the work it was built on. Backwards citation searching reaches the foundations of an argument.

_items.title: Citation searching, forwards
_items.body: Use a citation index to find later work that cites your key paper. Forwards citation searching reaches the debate that followed, including challenges to it.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two researchers search for literature on the same question.

{{learner-a}} runs a discovery-service search, skims the first two pages, saves a handful of results, and declares the search done. The list looks reasonable, so the gaps are invisible. {{learner-a}} has not noticed that the most-cited work in the field never appeared, because it sits in a specialist database the discovery service indexes poorly.

{{learner-b}} starts in the discovery service too, but treats it as the first stage. {{learner-b}} moves into a subject database for depth, then takes the strongest paper found and searches its reference list backwards to its foundations and a citation index forwards to later work that cites it. That citation trail surfaces two central sources the first search missed, and shows which claims the field has since challenged.

Both began with the same tool. Only {{learner-b}} extended the search far enough to be fair to the literature.

title: Practical guidance
displayTitle: Checklist: How to extend a search
body: Use these moves to push a search past the discovery service.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Have I treated the discovery service as a start rather than the whole search?
Have I searched at least one subject database for depth in my field?
Have I used the strongest source's reference list to search backwards?
Have I used a citation index to search forwards to later work?
Have I noticed any central work the first search did not return?
Can I say why my coverage is now wide enough to be fair to the debate?

title: Formative check: why coverage falls short
displayTitle: Why does a discovery-service search alone tend to leave gaps in coverage?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why does a discovery-service search alone leave gaps?

_items.text: It favours breadth, under-indexes specialist literature, and ranks by rules you do not control.
_items.feedback: Yes. Those are exactly the limits that make it a start, not a finish.

_items.text: It only ever returns sources that are too old to use.
_items.feedback: Age is not the issue; the gap is in depth and indexing, not currency.

_items.text: It refuses to show peer-reviewed research.
_items.feedback: It does show peer-reviewed work; it just under-indexes specialist databases.

_items.text: It returns too few results to be useful at all.
_items.feedback: It usually returns plenty; the problem is what it misses, not the quantity.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Breadth over depth, weak specialist indexing and uncontrolled ranking are its limits.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what the discovery service does less well than a specialist tool.
_incorrect.final: A discovery service leaves gaps because it favours breadth over depth, under-indexes specialist literature, and ranks by rules you do not control, not because results are too old or too few.

title: Formative check: extending the search
displayTitle: In the worked example, what did the second researcher do to extend the search beyond the discovery service?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What did the second researcher do to extend the search?

_items.text: Searched a subject database and followed a key paper's citations backwards and forwards.
_items.feedback: Yes. Databases plus citation trails reached what the first search missed.

_items.text: Ran the same discovery-service search a second time, more slowly.
_items.feedback: Repeating the same search does not extend its coverage.

_items.text: Saved more results from the first two pages of library results.
_items.feedback: Saving more of the same results does not reach new parts of the literature.

_items.text: Chose the most readable source from the original list.
_items.feedback: Readability is not coverage; this does not extend the search.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A subject database and citation searching, backwards and forwards, extended the coverage.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the moves that reached literature the discovery service did not surface.
_incorrect.final: The second researcher extended the search by using a subject database and following a key paper's citations backwards and forwards, not by repeating or re-reading the first search.

title: Formative check: following citations
displayTitle: In {{context}}, you have found a strong, highly relevant paper. Which move best extends your search through citation searching?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which move best extends your search through citation searching?

_items.text: Search its reference list backwards and a citation index forwards to find the work it builds on and the work that cites it.
_items.feedback: Yes. In {{context}}, that two-way citation trail maps the conversation around the paper.

_items.text: Read the paper again to be sure you have understood it.
_items.feedback: Understanding the paper is useful but does not extend the search.

_items.text: Add the paper to your list and stop searching, since it is strong.
_items.feedback: Stopping at one strong paper is the gap this lesson warns against.

_items.text: Look for a more recent paper on a loosely related topic.
_items.feedback: A loosely related paper is not citation searching and may not be relevant.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, following citations backwards and forwards extends the reach of the search.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option that follows the paper's citations in both directions.
_incorrect.final: In {{context}}, citation searching means following a strong paper's references backwards and its citations forwards, not re-reading it, stopping, or drifting to a loosely related topic.

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: The controls that steer a search
body: Read the passage and select each marked term to see what it does.
instruction: Select each highlighted term to reveal its definition.

_passage.text: A precise search is built, not stumbled upon. You combine your terms with

_term.definition: The words AND, OR and NOT that combine search terms. AND narrows a search to results containing both terms, OR widens it to either, and NOT excludes a term.
Placing quotation marks around words so the search treats them as a fixed phrase, for example "working memory", rather than as separate terms that may appear far apart.

_passage.text: , and catch a word's variants with

_term.definition: Adding a symbol, usually an asterisk, to a word stem so the search also finds its endings. For example, analy* returns analyse, analysis and analytical.

_passage.text: . You then narrow the results with

_term.definition: Filters that restrict results by date, source type, peer-review status, language and more. Limiters raise precision by removing material that does not fit your criteria.
How much of the relevant material a search captures. High recall means you miss little, usually at the cost of more irrelevant results to sift.
How little irrelevant material a search returns. High precision means a cleaner result set, usually at the cost of missing some relevant work.

_passage.text: . The balance is a judgement you revisit with each pass.
Two further controls refine the set.

_term.definition: Commands such as NEAR or ADJ that require two terms to appear within a set number of words of each other, so the search finds genuine relationships rather than terms that merely share a document.

_passage.text: require your terms to sit within a set distance of each other, catching real relationships that a loose AND would miss. Where a database offers them,

_term.definition: Standardised topic labels (controlled vocabulary) a database assigns to records, letting you search by concept rather than by the words an author chose, which catches relevant work that uses different phrasing.

_passage.text: let you search by an assigned topic rather than by the words an author happened to choose. Used together, these turn a broad sweep into a targeted search.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two researchers search the same database for the same topic.

{{learner-a}} types a long natural-language sentence into the search box and presses enter. The database returns many thousands of loosely related results, ranked by its own rules. {{learner-a}} scrolls through the first page, feels overwhelmed, and picks whatever looks closest. The search was wide, but it was never steered.

{{learner-b}} builds the search instead. Key concepts are joined with AND, synonyms gathered with OR, a set expression fixed in quotation marks, and a stem truncated to catch variants. {{learner-b}} then applies a date and a peer-review limiter, reads the first results, sees the net is still too wide, and tightens one term. Two passes later the result set is small, relevant and defensible.

Both searched the same database. Only {{learner-b}} controlled precision and recall, and refined the search as a cycle rather than a single try.

title: Practical guidance
displayTitle: Checklist: How to refine a search
body: Use these controls to steer what a search returns, then iterate.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Have I combined my terms with AND, OR and NOT deliberately?
Have I fixed any set expressions in quotation marks?
Have I truncated word stems to catch their variants?
Have I applied limiters to filter by date, type or peer review?
Have I decided whether this task needs more recall or more precision?
Have I read the results and refined the search at least once more?

title: Formative check: Boolean control
displayTitle: You want results that mention both of two concepts. Which Boolean operator should join them?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which Boolean operator requires both terms to be present?

_items.text: AND, which narrows the search to results containing both terms.
_items.feedback: Yes. AND requires both terms, narrowing the results.

_items.text: OR, which widens the search to results containing either term.
_items.feedback: OR widens to either term; it does not require both.

_items.text: NOT, which excludes a term from the results.
_items.feedback: NOT excludes a term; it does not combine two you want.

_items.text: Quotation marks, which fix a phrase rather than combine concepts.
_items.feedback: Quotation marks keep words together as a phrase; they are not a Boolean operator for two concepts.

_feedback.correct: That's right. AND narrows a search to results that contain both terms.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which operator requires both terms to be present?
_incorrect.final: AND narrows a search to results containing both terms. OR widens to either, NOT excludes, and quotation marks fix a phrase rather than combining two concepts.

title: Formative check: precision and recall
displayTitle: In the worked example, what did the second researcher do that the first did not?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What did the second researcher do that the first did not?

_items.text: Built the search with Boolean logic, phrases, truncation and limiters, then refined it over more than one pass.
_items.feedback: Yes. That is controlling precision and recall and iterating.

_items.text: Typed a longer natural-language sentence into the search box.
_items.feedback: A longer sentence is what the first researcher did; it does not steer the search.

_items.text: Picked the first result that looked close enough.
_items.feedback: That is the weaker approach, not the controlled one.

_items.text: Accepted the database's default ranking without change.
_items.feedback: Leaving the ranking untouched is not refining the search.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Building the search with operators and limiters and refining it is deliberate control.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option that steers the search and revisits it.
_incorrect.final: The second researcher built the search with Boolean logic, phrases, truncation and limiters and refined it over several passes, rather than typing a long sentence or accepting the default results.

title: Formative check: iterating the search
displayTitle: Your first search in {{context}} returns thousands of loosely related results. What does this lesson recommend you do next?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What should you do when a first search returns thousands of loosely related results?

_items.text: Tighten the search with narrower terms or a limiter, run it again, and keep refining until the balance is right.
_items.feedback: Yes. In {{context}}, refinement is an iterative cycle, not a single try.

_items.text: Work through all the results in order until you find enough.
_items.feedback: Wading through everything ignores the controls that would sharpen the search.

_items.text: Abandon the topic because the literature is too large.
_items.feedback: A large result set is a signal to refine, not to give up.

_items.text: Keep the results as they are, since a wide search is always better.
_items.feedback: A wide search with low precision is not better; balance is the goal.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, you tighten, re-run and keep refining until precision and recall are balanced.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. A huge result set is a signal to do what to the search?
_incorrect.final: In {{context}}, a huge, loosely related result set is a signal to tighten the search and iterate, not to read everything, give up, or leave a low-precision search as it is.

body: Which of these is the best account of evaluating a source rigorously?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which account best describes evaluating a source rigorously?

_items.text: Weighing source type, currency, authority and relevance against your question, and justifying the call.
_items.feedback: Yes. That is rigorous evaluation.

_items.text: Choosing the most recent source available.
_items.feedback: Recency is one criterion, not the whole judgement.

_items.text: Keeping every source you find, to be safe.
_items.feedback: Evaluation means choosing with reasons, not keeping everything.

_items.text: Trusting a source because it appears in the library.
_items.feedback: Catalogue presence is not an appraisal.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Evaluation weighs the criteria against your question and justifies the choice.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about weighing several criteria, not a single one.

body: A recent, well-written news article summarises a technical research claim. For an argument that needs authority, how should you treat it?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: How should you treat a news article summarising a research claim when you need authority?

_items.text: As weak on authority for the claim, and trace it to the peer-reviewed study it summarises.
_items.feedback: Yes. Its type and authority are thin for a technical claim.

_items.text: As ideal, because it is recent and clearly written.
_items.feedback: Recency and readability do not supply authority.

_items.text: As authoritative, because it has been published.
_items.feedback: Publication as journalism does not give authority for a research claim.

_items.text: As irrelevant, and ignore it entirely.
_items.feedback: It can still be useful for context; the point is not to rely on it for authority.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Judge its type and authority, and go to the study behind it.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. What do source type and authority say about a news summary of research?

body: Why is a discovery-service search, on its own, usually not enough for thorough coverage?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why is a discovery-service search alone usually not enough for thorough coverage?

_items.text: It favours breadth over depth and under-indexes specialist databases.
_items.feedback: Yes. That is why you extend into databases and citation trails.

_items.text: It only returns sources that are behind paywalls.
_items.feedback: Access is not the issue; depth and indexing are.

_items.text: It never returns academic sources.
_items.feedback: It does return academic sources; it just misses specialist depth.

_items.text: It ranks results alphabetically by author.
_items.feedback: Its ranking is relevance-based and opaque, not alphabetical.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Breadth over depth and weak specialist indexing leave gaps.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about depth versus breadth.

body: What is forwards citation searching?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What is forwards citation searching?

_items.text: Using a citation index to find later work that cites a key paper.
_items.feedback: Yes. Forwards means later work that cites the paper.

_items.text: Reading a paper's own reference list.
_items.feedback: That is backwards citation searching.

_items.text: Re-running a search with more recent date limits.
_items.feedback: A date limit is not citation searching.

_items.text: Searching for the paper's title in a general web search.
_items.feedback: A title search is not following citations.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Forwards citation searching finds the later work that cites a paper.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which direction reaches the work that came after?

body: You join two search terms with OR. What is the effect?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What is the effect of joining two search terms with OR?

_items.text: The search widens to results containing either term.
_items.feedback: Yes. OR broadens a search and raises recall.

_items.text: The search narrows to results containing both terms.
_items.feedback: That is AND, not OR.

_items.text: The search excludes both terms from the results.
_items.feedback: That is closer to NOT, and NOT excludes one term.

_items.text: The two terms are treated as a single fixed phrase.
_items.feedback: That is what quotation marks do, not OR.

_feedback.correct: That's right. OR widens a search to either term, raising recall.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Does OR require both terms, or either?

body: A search returns far too many loosely related results. Which move raises precision?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which move raises precision when a search returns too many loosely related results?

_items.text: Apply limiters and narrow the terms, then re-run and refine.
_items.feedback: Yes. Limiters and tighter terms raise precision, and you iterate.

_items.text: Replace AND with OR to gather even more results.
_items.feedback: OR widens the search and lowers precision.

_items.text: Remove all limiters so nothing is filtered out.
_items.feedback: Removing limiters lowers precision further.

_items.text: Read every result in the order returned.
_items.feedback: That ignores the controls that would sharpen the search.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Limiters and narrower terms raise precision, and refinement is iterative.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which move removes irrelevant results rather than adding more?

title: Orientation
body: You have now looked at three things: evaluating sources against explicit criteria, extending a search past the discovery service, and refining a search for precision and recall. On their own they are three separate techniques. This lesson brings them together into one practice you can keep using.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this level you can already do each of these on its own. The aim now is to see them as one practice rather than three separate techniques, so that searching well carries on through the rest of your studies.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: bring together evaluating sources, extending a search, and refining for precision and recall into one search practice
recognise this one search practice at work in a researcher's ongoing study
plan how you will keep searching well in your {{context}} study beyond this course

title: Concept: definition
body: Searching well is those three strands working as one. You reach widely, extending past the discovery service into databases and citation trails. You control what comes back, refining for precision and recall. You judge each source against explicit criteria of type, currency, authority and relevance. It is not three separate techniques but one practice you run, and defend, every time you research.

title: Concept: in practice
body: In practice this is something you do on every piece of research, not once. You reach past the library's first results into databases and citation trails, then control the search so it is sharp enough to be useful. You weigh each source you find against explicit criteria, and you repeat the cycle until the set is both fair and defensible. Each search teaches you how to run the next one better.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of a piece of research you have coming up in your own subject. How will you reach widely, sharpen the search, and judge what you find, and when will you stop and refine again?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and the questions have no right answers.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: Searching well is most useful as a continuing practice. You reach widely, refine for precision and recall, and judge each source against criteria, again and again across your research. It is the practice, not any single search, that makes your work both fair and defensible.

title: The practice as one cycle
displayTitle: The practice as one cycle
body: Searching well is one continuing practice, run and defended every time you research. Select each part to see what it involves.
instruction: Select each part of the cycle.

_items.title: Reach widely
_items.body: Reach widely, extending past the discovery service into subject databases and citation trails.

_items.title: Control
_items.body: Control what comes back, refining the search with Boolean logic, phrases, truncation and limiters for precision and recall.

_items.title: Judge
_items.body: Judge the results, weighing each source against type, currency, authority and relevance.

_items.title: Iterate and defend
_items.body: Iterate, running the cycle again as needed, and defend every source you keep or set aside. The cycle keeps turning.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body: Two students research the same question. One runs a single discovery-service search, takes the first few results, and uses them without asking how good they are. The other reaches into a subject database and a citation trail, tightens the search for precision and recall, and judges each source against explicit criteria before keeping it. Over the term, the second student's work rests on sources that are both well chosen and defensible, because searching became one practice rather than three separate techniques.

title: Working with the cycle
displayTitle: Checklist: How to keep searching well
body: Use these questions on a search you are running, to keep the three strands working together.
instruction: Tick each item when you have done it.

_items.text: Did I reach past the discovery service into databases and citation trails?
Did I control the search with Boolean logic, phrases, truncation and limiters?
Did I judge each source against type, currency, authority and relevance?
Did I treat the search as a cycle I repeat, not a single pass?
Can I justify, in a sentence, every source I kept and every one I set aside?

displayTitle: Why is it more useful to treat evaluating, extending and refining as one search practice rather than three separate techniques?
body: Why is it more useful to treat evaluating, extending and refining as one search practice rather than three separate techniques?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why is it more useful to treat evaluating, extending and refining as one search practice rather than three separate techniques?

_items.text: Because each strand feeds the others: how widely you reach shapes what you must refine, and what you refine shapes what you then judge.
_items.feedback: Yes. The three strands support each other, so they work best as one practice.

_items.text: Because getting one of the three right means you can skip the other two.
_items.feedback: Each strand needs the others; none of them stands on its own.

_items.text: Because treating it as one practice means you never have to evaluate what you find.
_items.feedback: Evaluating sources is one of the three strands, not something the practice removes.

_items.text: Because one practice takes less thought than reaching, refining and judging separately.
_items.feedback: It is not about less thought. The strands simply work better together than apart.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The three strands feed each other, so searching works best as one practice.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about how reaching widely, refining and judging depend on each other.

displayTitle: A student searches a subject database and a citation trail, tightens the search with Boolean operators and a limiter, then weighs each result against explicit criteria. What does this show?
body: A student searches a subject database and a citation trail, tightens the search with Boolean operators and a limiter, then weighs each result against explicit criteria. What does this show?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A student searches a subject database and a citation trail, tightens the search with Boolean operators and a limiter, then weighs each result against explicit criteria. What does this show?

_items.text: That the three strands are running as one practice: reaching widely, controlling the search, and judging what it returns.
_items.feedback: Yes. Extend, refine and evaluate worked together as one connected practice.

_items.text: That only one of the three moves was needed, and the others were wasted.
_items.feedback: Each move did real work: reaching, refining and judging all mattered.

_items.text: That evaluating what you find can replace searching widely in the first place.
_items.feedback: Reaching widely is a strand in its own right, not something evaluation removes.

_items.text: That the search is now finished and need never be repeated.
_items.feedback: Searching well is a cycle you repeat, not a single pass.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Reaching widely, refining the search and judging the results ran together as one practice.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look at the three kinds of move the student made, and how they fit together.

displayTitle: You want to use this one search practice to research {{context}} better this term. Which plan best brings the three strands together?
body: You want to use this one search practice to research {{context}} better this term. Which plan best brings the three strands together?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: You want to use this one search practice to research your subject better this term. Which plan best brings the three strands together?

_items.text: For each search, reach past the discovery service, control it for precision and recall, then judge every source against criteria, and repeat.
_items.feedback: Yes. That runs all three strands together, again and again, as one practice.

_items.text: Pick one of the three strands and rely on it for every {{context}} search.
_items.feedback: The strands work together; relying on one leaves the others undone.

_items.text: Take the first page of discovery-service results for {{context}} and trust it as it is.
_items.feedback: That skips reaching widely, refining and judging, which is the whole practice.

_items.text: Reach as widely as you can in {{context}}, but never narrow or evaluate what returns.
_items.feedback: Reaching widely only helps if you then refine the search and judge what it finds.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Running all three strands on each search keeps the practice going across your {{context}} work.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the plan that reaches, refines and judges together, again and again.

title: Summative item 7 (tests co4)
displayTitle: Searching well brings three strands together. Which description captures how they work as one practice?
body: Searching well brings three strands together. Which description captures how they work as one practice?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Searching well brings three strands together. Which description captures how they work as one practice?

_items.text: You reach past the discovery service, control the search for precision and recall, and judge each source against explicit criteria.
_items.feedback: Yes. The three strands run as one connected practice.

_items.text: You take the first results a discovery service returns and use them as they come.
_items.feedback: That skips the reaching, refining and judging that make up the practice.

_items.text: You reach as widely as possible and never narrow or evaluate the results.
_items.feedback: Reaching widely is only one strand; refining and judging are needed too.

_items.text: You judge sources carefully but never search beyond the discovery service.
_items.feedback: Judging well still needs a search that reaches widely and is refined.

_feedback.correct: Correct.

title: Summative item 8 (tests co4)
displayTitle: A student extends a search into two databases and a citation trail, tightens it with Boolean operators and a date limiter, then weighs each result against currency and authority before deciding what to keep. Which strands is she using?
body: A student extends a search into two databases and a citation trail, tightens it with Boolean operators and a date limiter, then weighs each result against currency and authority before deciding what to keep. Which strands is she using?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A student extends a search into two databases and a citation trail, tightens it with Boolean operators and a date limiter, then weighs each result against currency and authority before deciding what to keep. Which strands is she using?

_items.text: All three: she extends the search, refines it for precision, and evaluates what it returns.
_items.feedback: Yes. She moves through all three strands as one practice.

_items.text: Only extending the search; she has not refined or evaluated anything.
_items.feedback: She also tightened the search and weighed the results, so more than one strand is at work.

_items.text: None; using databases and limiters is not part of searching well.
_items.feedback: Databases, limiters and evaluation are exactly the strands of searching well.

_items.text: Only evaluating sources; the searching itself plays no part.
_items.feedback: She extended and refined the search too, so the searching is central.

_feedback.correct: Correct.
